questions.question: Distinguish population distribution from population density, and explain South Africa's population pattern using both physical and human factors.
questions.expected_answer: Population distribution describes where people are — the pattern of their spread, in words like clustered or dispersed — while population density measures how many, calculated as total population divided by total area in people per square kilometre; and density is an average that can flatten reality, as Egypt shows, where a moderate national figure hides near-total crowding along the Nile. South Africa's pattern reflects physical factors first: rainfall declines from over 1 000 millimetres on the eastern escarpment to under 100 in the west, so population thickens eastward, and the arid Northern Cape — the largest province — carries only about 2 people per square kilometre because farming is nearly impossible. But human factors override physical ones where history demands: Gauteng, the smallest province, holds roughly a quarter of the population on the dry Highveld because the Witwatersrand gold discoveries of 1886 pulled labour, railways and industry there; the coastal metros of Cape Town, Durban and Gqeberha grew on harbours and trade; and apartheid's homeland system concentrated millions on marginal rural land, a legacy still visible in the Eastern Cape and Limpopo.

questions.question: Explain how a population pyramid is read, describe the demographic transition behind its changing shape, and comment on the particular features of South Africa's pyramid.
questions.expected_answer: A pyramid stacks horizontal age bars from newborns at the base to the aged at the apex, males left and females right, and is read in three looks: the base for the birth rate, the slope of the sides for survival, and the top for longevity. A wide-based triangle with fast-narrowing sides and an empty top marks a young, fast-growing developing population with high birth rate, high infant mortality and heavy youth dependency; a slim-based column with straight sides and a broad top marks a developed, ageing population with low births, long lives and rising aged dependency. The demographic transition model explains the journey between the shapes: in stage one both vital rates are high and growth minimal; in stage two the death rate falls with clean water, vaccines and food while births stay high, so population explodes; in stage three the birth rate follows down as children survive and women gain education and contraception; in stage four both rates are low and population stabilises; and in stage five, visible in Japan and much of Europe, births fall below deaths and the population shrinks and ages. South Africa's pyramid is transitional: still youthful but with a narrowing base as fertility fell toward roughly 2.3 children per woman, and scarred by the HIV and Aids pandemic, which cut into the young-adult bars and dropped life expectancy through the 2000s before the world's largest treatment programme turned it upward again.

questions.question: Explain why South Africa is described as a dry country, how it nonetheless suffers deadly floods, and what water management requires from government, agriculture and households.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa averages about 464 millimetres of rain a year against a world average near 860, ranking among the thirty driest countries; the rain falls unevenly — generous in the east, meagre in the west — and unreliably, with high evaporation, so two-thirds of the country receives less than the 500 millimetres needed for rain-fed cropping. The answers are engineering — major dams like Gariep, inter-basin transfers led by the Lesotho Highlands Water Project supplying Gauteng, and boreholes into groundwater in the arid west. Floods still strike because intense convectional storms, cut-off lows and tropical moisture can overwhelm catchments primed by steep slopes and saturated or baked soil; human choices convert floods into disasters when cities seal the ground so runoff races off tar and roofs, wetlands are drained, and settlement — especially informal settlement — occupies floodplains, as Laingsburg 1981 and KwaZulu-Natal in April 2022 showed; on the hydrograph, degraded or sealed catchments draw the short lag and high narrow peak of a flashy river. Management spans three fronts: government must deliver the constitutional promise through the free basic water allowance of 6 000 litres per household per month, maintain pipes that currently lose about a third of municipal water, and protect wetlands and catchments; agriculture, using nearly two-thirds of the water, must adopt drip irrigation, lined canals and scheduling; and households and industry must fix leaks, harvest rainwater, recycle and accept tariffs that price waste while protecting the poor — with Cape Town's 2018 Day Zero near-miss as the standing warning.
